passage: Friday. Nirmala's diary. Today in Tenzin's class I forgot to look at Sir when he signed, and looked at my book instead. Tenzin tapped my shoulder twice and waited. I felt hot because it seemed rude, but he only smiled and pointed at his eyes. He explained that in sign language you keep looking at the signer's hands and face the whole time, and looking away means you are not listening. Then he flicked the lights to get everyone's attention when Mr Rao came in. It's clever! Tomorrow I'm going to keep my eyes up even when my pencil drops. 🙂

qa.q: How did Tenzin get Nirmala's attention?
qa.a: Tenzin tapped Nirmala's shoulder twice and waited.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when Tenzin tapped Nirmala's shoulder, and what did Nirmala learn?
qa.a: Nirmala felt embarrassed, thinking it was rude, shown by feeling hot. Then Nirmala learned that keeping eyes on the signer is expected, not an insult.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do next time Nirmala's pencil drops during a signed lesson?
qa.a: Nirmala could keep watching the signer, then pick the pencil up at a pause or ask quietly by signing 'wait' before looking away.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Nirmala's mistake?
qa.a: Tenzin is kind about it. Tenzin smiles and points to the eyes, treating it as something Nirmala has not learned yet.

grounding: A young learner discovers that visual attention and turn-taking, like tapping and flicking lights, are respectful and required in signing.

passage: The village school at Sundarpur had one hearing teacher and Wasim, a deaf Class 6 boy, at the third bench. Devika, ten, had just moved to the village. When the teacher began to explain fractions, Devika saw that Wasim's eyes never left the interpreter's hands. When the teacher called him, she waved to get his attention, and he turned with a smile. At break she said, "Why do you stare at her so much?" Wasim signed slowly, and the interpreter translated: "It is how I listen." Devika nodded. "Then I'll wave before I talk."

qa.q: Which bench did Wasim sit at?
qa.a: He sat at the third bench.

qa.q: What did Devika probably feel when Wasim explained why he stared at the interpreter, and what other reaction is possible?
qa.a: She probably felt understanding and a little embarrassed for asking. She might also have felt a bit unsure about how to talk to him, though she decided on waving first.

qa.q: What could Devika do to be a good friend to Wasim?
qa.a: She could wave or tap gently before speaking, look at him when he signs, and learn a few signs so they can talk directly.

qa.q: What might it be like for Wasim when a new classmate asks about his staring?
qa.a: He may be patient since he explained in his own language. He might feel glad she listens, or tired of explaining again.

grounding: A signer keeps eye gaze on the signer's hands and face, and a new classmate learns to gain attention by waving.

passage:
Jana had just moved in next door to Siddiq's family in Berlin. The first time Siddiq signed to her, Jana looked down at the floor, trying to be polite. Siddiq stopped and waved his hand gently in front of her face.
She looked up. He signed again, slower, and this time she watched his hands, then his face. She didn't understand much, but he smiled.
The next day, Jana saw Siddiq's mother tap his shoulder to get his attention. At dinner his little brother flicked the kitchen lights, and everyone turned to him at once.
"I thought staring was rude," Jana told her own mother later. "But for them, looking is listening."
The next time Siddiq signed, Jana kept her eyes on his hands and face the whole way through.

qa.q: How did Siddiq's little brother get everyone's attention at dinner?
qa.a: He flicked the kitchen lights, and everyone turned to him at once.

qa.q: Why did Jana look down at the floor at first?
qa.a: She wanted to be polite and was probably shy and unsure, because where she came from staring felt rude; she did not yet know that for a signer, looking away can seem like not listening.

qa.q: What helped Jana change how she paid attention?
qa.a: Watching how Siddiq's family tapped shoulders, flicked lights and all turned to look showed her that watching the signer is the respectful way to listen.

qa.q: How might Siddiq have felt when Jana first looked at the floor?
qa.a: He might have felt ignored or puzzled, since in his family looking at hands and face is how people listen.

grounding: A child learns that signers get attention by waving, tapping or flicking lights, and that keeping eyes on the signer is respectful.

passage:
In the mixed class at the Pune school, Mrs Kale asked everyone to answer in turn. Tanuja, who is Deaf, had her hand up, but the hearing children kept talking over each other.
She reached over and flicked the classroom light switch twice. Everyone turned, startled.
Yash frowned. "Why did she do that?" he whispered.
The interpreter signed to Tanuja and answered him quietly: "That's how signers get a group's attention. Like calling out, but for eyes."
Tanuja began signing her answer. Yash kept staring at the interpreter, then noticed Tanuja glancing at his face, checking. He moved his eyes to her hands and face instead.
At the end, Tanuja caught his eye and smiled. Yash signed "thank you" clumsily. She laughed and showed him the right way.

qa.q: How many times did Tanuja flick the light switch?
qa.a: She flicked it twice.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the lights flicked?
qa.a: Yash felt startled and confused, and perhaps a little annoyed, because he did not yet know flicking lights is a normal way for a signer to get attention.

qa.q: How could a teacher help the hearing children take turns fairly with Tanuja?
qa.a: Mrs Kale could explain the light flick and waving beforehand, stop talk-overs, and remind everyone to watch the signer's hands and face during her turn.

qa.q: If you were Tanuja, what would you want from the class?
qa.a: You would want people to notice your raised hand without needing the lights, and to look at you rather than only at the interpreter while you answer.

grounding: A classroom shows a Deaf child getting attention by flicking lights, and a hearing classmate learning to keep his gaze on the signer.

passage:
At Sunday lunch, my Deaf cousin Amandeep sat next to me at Biji's big table. Whenever Amandeep wanted to say something, he waved a hand up high. The whole table turned and watched his hands and face, even Biji with a roti half-folded.
I used to think staring was rude, so I kept looking at my dal. Amandeep tapped my shoulder twice and waited till I looked up.
Then he signed a story about my Chacha snoring on the train. I understood only the snoring part, but everyone laughed, and Chacha threw a napkin at him.
Amandeep was grinning so wide that I laughed too.
Now when he waves, I turn straight away and keep my eyes on him until he finishes.
- Tushar

qa.q: Where did the narrator keep looking at first?
qa.a: At the dal.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have been feeling when he tapped Tushar's shoulder?
qa.a: Amandeep may have felt a little left out or impatient that one listener was not watching, and wanted Tushar included in the story; he might also just have been eager to share the joke.

qa.q: What small step helps Tushar show respect now?
qa.a: Turning straight away when Amandeep waves and keeping eyes on his hands and face until he finishes.

qa.q: How might Chacha feel about being the subject of the snoring story?
qa.a: Chacha seems amused rather than hurt, since everyone laughed and he playfully threw a napkin at Amandeep.

grounding: An observer at a family lunch learns that a signer waves or taps for attention and that watching hands and face is respectful.

passage:
Saturday: Manoj called "Sarika!" three times across the courtyard. His cousin kept patting her sandcastle. Manoj scowled. "She's ignoring me." Sarika's mother touched his arm. "She's Deaf, beta. Wave where she can see you, or tap her shoulder."
Sunday: Manoj tapped Sarika's shoulder and she turned, smiling. She signed slowly for him, but when a shout came from the cricket in the street, Manoj glanced away. Sarika stopped mid-sign and waited. Manoj went red. Looking away meant he had stopped listening.
The next Saturday: At dusk, Manoj flicked the veranda light off and on. Sarika looked up at once. This time he kept his eyes on her hands and face through her whole story, and nodded when she finished.

qa.q: How did Manoj get Sarika's attention the next Saturday?
qa.a: He flicked the veranda light off and on.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he said Sarika was ignoring him?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and a bit hurt, believing she was ignoring him, when she simply couldn't hear his calls.

qa.q: Which change made their conversations work?
qa.a: Getting attention in a way Sarika could see, then keeping his eyes on her hands and face the whole time, which is how she needs to be listened to 👍

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika when Manoj glances away mid-sign?
qa.a: For Sarika it is like someone turning away while you talk, so she stopped and waited until he was watching again.

grounding: It shows a child learning that a Deaf signer is reached by waving, a tap or a light flick, and that keeping eyes on the hands and face is how you listen.
